utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Michelle Jarvis appearing for the Prosecution this morning. Mr. Stringer has conveyed his apologies to the Court. He is unable to be present. I'm appearing today with Elizabeth Spelman and our case manager, Indah Susanti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with Cory Stevens, legal assistant, and Amilee Myson, legal intern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May the record reflect that the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Hall being absent. The hearing today arises from a proprio motu order of the Trial Chamber issued on the 1st of April, 2015, ordering the appointment of independent experts to assist the Trial Chamber in determining whether Mr. Hadzic is fit to stand trial. The aim of this hearing is to have the appointed independent expert, Mr. Martell, answer questions from the Prosecution, the Defence, and possibly the Chamber, to provide further explanations and clarifications regarding his expert report filed on 23 July 2015. Today's hearing will begin with 45 minutes of questioning from the Prosecution, followed by 45 minutes of questioning from the Defence, and conclude with Chamber's questions, if any. I would like now to ask the parties' submissions with regard to the character of this hearing. I do remember that the previous expert hearing was, at the end, decided to be public. Today's hearing is perhaps a little bit more delicate so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What would the Defence -- what would the position be for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The position from the Defence is that there is no objection to public session for the content of the testimony. With the exception of any discussion of the final prognosis. As Your Honours know, the specificity in terms of the amount of time that is mentioned in the final prognosis, we have redacted that in all of our submissions. So we would just request that in respect of that item, that that be kept in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Any position from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will stay in public session and try to avoid and eventually intervene on -- to avoid in public session the issue raised by the Defence and eventually intervene. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Martell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to thank you as we start this hearing for your willingness to assist the Tribunal on a very short notice in Serbia and now in The Hague. For the record, would you please state your name, your date of birth, and your profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Daniel Martell. I was born October 22nd, 1957, and I am a forensic neuropsychologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Martell. Although I know you are perfectly familiar with what I am go to say, I have to point out that by making the solemn declaration I will ask you to read, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, you may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Dr. Martell - and this is also for OTP and the Defence - may I ask you to speak slowly and pause between questions and answers because everything that is said has to be translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Jarvis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My name is Elizabeth Spelman on behalf --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: -- of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Spelman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: If I may ask, at the end of my questions if I have any time left over, I respectively request that I can use that time, please, for any follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: So good morning, Dr. Martell.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: As I said, my name is Elizabeth Spelman and I'm a lawyer for the Prosecution here at the Tribunal, and I have some questions about the report that you've prepared on the basis of the Chamber's request. Can I just check, do you have a copy of that report with you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: In the course of my questions if there's anything at all that you would like me to clarify, please do not hesitate to let me know. So can I ask what were the exact terms of your instructions from the Tribunal in carrying out your examination of Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I was asked to carry out an in-depth testing that would assist the Trial Chamber in determining whether Mr. Hadzic is fit to stand trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And did the Registry provide you with an explanation of the ICTY standard of fitness for trial?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: I understand that you examined Mr. Hadzic over the course of two days, on the 13th and 14th of July, 2015, in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: How long did the entire examination last?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: The first day, I was with him from approximately 9.00 in the morning until noon. At that time he became too tired to continue. I gave him a test called the MMPI, which is short for Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory. It's a paper and pencil test that would take him several hours to complete. I asked him to have his lunch and take his nap and then complete the test in the afternoon. I came back the next morning at 9.00 and saw him again until about noon that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And so how many hours in total would you say the examination lasted?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I spent approximately six hours face to face with him and he spent approximately another three hours out of my presence completing the MMPI-2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And did Mr. Hadzic understand the reason for your examination of him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And you were confident that he had no difficulty in understanding that he had to provide his consent and that the examination or the results of the examination would not remain private between you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that Mr. Hadzic gave his informed consent to the examination that you conducted?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: As can you see, Mr. Hadzic is not here today and he has provided his written consent for today's hearing to proceed in his absence. Do you think that Mr. Hadzic understood what he was doing when he signed the relevant waiver?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: He did not sign a waiver. He provided a verbal indication that he understood the reason for the examination and that he consented to participate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thanks, Dr. Martell. I should perhaps just explain myself a little bit better. Mr. Hadzic is not here today at this hearing and as a result of not being here he signed a waiver saying that he wouldn't be here. And do you think that he understood what he was doing when he signed that waiver?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Dr. Martell doesn't know what Mr. Hadzic's condition was at the time that he signed this document. Dr. Martell has no knowledge of when the document was signed. Dr. Martell doesn't know the content of the document. In these circumstances it's a question that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honours, if I may rephrase the question then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Martell, based on the time that you spent with Mr. Hadzic and your examinations of him, do you think that he had the capability to understand the implications of signing the waiver today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. Again, Mr. President, Dr. Martell doesn't know the content of the waiver, doesn't know the circumstances of it being signed. He cannot answer the question as posed without speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'll allow the question. Please answer the question, if you can, Mr. Martell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would suppose, and there are some suppositions, that he understood that signing the waiver meant that he would not have to leave Novi Sad and come attend this proceeding, and I think he is capable of understanding that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Martell. During the examination you asked Mr. Hadzic both oral and written questions.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: How many oral questions approximately did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And how many written questions did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's pretty exact. Thank you. And was the questioning or were the tests, were they conducted under conditions that were designed to be stressful?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: No, but they can be for some people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And do you find that subjects perhaps who are being assessed, do they perform better when the conditions are not stressful?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: My objective is to extract the best possible performance from the person I'm examining. I do whatever it takes to make them comfortable and to make the testing as straightforward for them as possible. Given whatever deficits or limitations a patient may have, they may find the testing stressful as they realise things that they can't do and that may be difficult for them. But, in general, I try to make it as unstressful as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And were Mr. Hadzic's answers responsive to the questions that you posed?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: In your report you mention that you worked with an interpreter and you asked her to alert to you any abnormal word pronunciations and wrong or atypical word choices. Did she have to do this on many occasions?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: No, only on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And when you say "a couple," is it approximately two or more?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I would say approximately two, maybe three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that Mr. Hadzic had difficulty maintaining attention after approximately two and a half hours. For how long approximately could he maintain attention without becoming tired or requiring a break?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Well, these are two different questions. He has some fairly severe problems with attention, with paying attention to what's happening around him, and he also becomes fatigued after approximately two and a half hours of sustained focused activity. Now, for example, sitting through my testing, at the end of about two and a half hours his performance would drop off. He was less able to interact with me. He became more uncomfortable. He needed to sleep. During that time, he displayed problems with attention but he also has the lack of stamina to continue beyond that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned that he took some breaks. How long approximately were those breaks?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: We took short breaks for the restroom, and then at the end of about two and a half hours, he could not tolerate any additional testing and needed to stop to sleep. He told me that he would generally sleep for anywhere from half an hour to an hour and a half and that that would "recharge his battery."

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And after the break did you find that Mr. Hadzic could focus again on your questions?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I saw him the next day. I did not remain in his apartment while he napped. I gave him the paper and pencil test to take. I saw him the next morning and he was a little different than the first day. He found it very difficult to complete the 567 questions on the test and felt that that took a lot of his energy the previous afternoon and evening. And that morning, the next morning, he was less able to focus and engage in the testing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss Mr. Hadzic's medical history with him; for example, did you discuss his treatment and the medication that he is receiving?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss it any particular detail or did you rely mostly on the information that you were provided with?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I found the medical record to be more informative than Mr. Hadzic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you speak at length about his medical history?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And did you discuss any other topics; such as, did you discuss his family?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And any past events? For example, how he came to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Well, he did mention that there was a period of time when he was in hiding from the Tribunal, but I did not spend time talking about his case in chief because I felt that was outside of my referral question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of this -- of these discussions, however, can you just provide me some more details about your discussion with him. What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I took a history from him. He told me a bit -- he -- in terms of his medical history he was concerned that I understand about his falls at the United Nations Detention Centre. He particularly wanted me to understand he felt that on his first fall he had dislocated his shoulder and that the doctors at the facility, in attempting to reset the shoulder, had in fact broken his arm. And I did not see that in the medical record but that was his understanding of what happened and he wanted me to know that that was what happened. He was able to tell me his parents' names, the work that they did, he was able to tell me where he was born. He was able to tell me how far he went in school. He was able to tell me about his everyday functioning, his sleeping, his eating, problems he had noticed in his thinking and his memory. And he was able to give me at least a brief overview of his psychiatric and medical history.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And you mention that he discussed with you his time on the run.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you provide any more detail than that?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: No, he just alluded to the fact that he had spent time on the run. He also spent some time talking about religious ideas that he has and spiritual feelings that he has. And I offered that -- and that he had read hundreds of books about religion. And I offered to him that perhaps he had read those while he was hiding in the monastery, which I had read from the internet, and he actually denied that and -- not that he had been there but that he read the books from the monastery, and he argued that his faith was larger than that of the priests.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of those books, did he say -- did he -- just from what you said there, was that he read them recently or was it --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I think that he had read them over his lifetime and particularly the last seven or eight years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you discuss him time in the UN Detention Unit with you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Only in small bits. The incidents where he fell and the incident with his broken arm. He also described a hallucinatory experience that he had during his chemotherapy treatment where he thought he saw a shadow walk through his door that he believed to be his father. That this happened five or six times. He attributed this to his chemotherapy. He said he was having other symptoms. He described it like a laser show going off in his room, that he was nauseous, that he was dizzy, that he felt it was side effects. It had never happened before and it did not happen again after.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention that he wanted to be quite sure in explaining to you the details of his shoulder injury. Did he engage or try to initiate any other kind of discussion with you which you hadn't initiated?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: He did talk some. I'd asked him about family history and he talked about being alienated from his first wife and the discomfort that that causes him in trying to think about planning for his last days and his estate and not wanting people fighting between his new family and his old family. It wasn't necessarily something he volunteered, but it was outside the scope of any direct question that I asked him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you arrive at any conclusions about Mr. Hadzic's medium and long-term memory?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: What were those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: His long-term memory is better than his short-term and intermediate memory. He is extremely impaired with regard to his short-term memory, but he was better able to discuss things that had happened in his past.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And how did you examine his medium and long-term memory?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Medium memory largely from the testing that I did. I administered a specialised computer-administered test in Serbian to him called the CNSVS, or Central Nervous System Vital Signs. That tests both his visual and his verbal memory, both immediate and short term, medium term. And so that's my primary instrument for shorter term memory. And long-term, like years and years memory, I did that based on interview and his ability to recount for me facts from his past.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss the nature of the charges against Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss the reason for his arrest and for his detention?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Based on your having spent two days with Mr. Hadzic, do you think that he has the ability or the capability to understand the charges against him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss the stage that the trial proceedings in this case are at with him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hadzic mention that he is currently on provisional release from the UN Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I was aware of that from the records, but did he not mention that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hadzic mention that he already testified in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Hadzic whether he understands that the Judges will determine whether he is responsible for the crimes for which is he charged?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: But, again, based on your having spent two days with Mr. Hadzic, do you think that he understands that he is involved in a trial and that he has proceedings against him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Prosecution has proposed modifications to the trial proceedings that would mean that Mr. Hadzic would not have to physically attend court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Would it have made a difference to your assessment of Mr. Hadzic's ability to participate in court proceedings if you knew that Mr. Hadzic did not have to attend the court proceedings or that the court proceedings could be modified to accommodate his needs for breaks and for sleep?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: But would it have made a difference to your assessment, do you think, about his ability to participate in court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: In what way would it have made a difference to your assessment?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Well, I think such accommodations would be critical for him to be involved at all with regard to his need for rest and his lack of physical endurance. I'm a bit confused, you know, about whether he would have the opportunity to observe the proceedings, and if that's relevant to the Court that he be able to do so. I think it's in that realm that I have greater concern about his fitness. But I do agree that shorter court days and accommodations for his physical disabilities would advance his fitness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And do you think -- yes, sorry. I'll just withdraw the question. That's fine. Thank you. So if I can just clarify some parts of your report, if that's okay, please, Dr. Martell.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: On page 8 of your report, you say regarding Mr. Hadzic that his insight was good. Can you explain to me what you meant by this, please.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: "Insight" is a term that we use in behavioural science to reflect the degree to which a person understands what's wrong with them and how it affects them. He has good insight into his illness and into the problems that it causes in his life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You say that specifically in relation to his illness. Do you think that is applicable to other issues?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Do you think he has a good insight or understanding of other matters in his life, not just his medical condition?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I do. He certainly has insight into the fact that his life is very limited at this point. He has insight into the ramifications of that for his family members that will survive him. He has insight into the fact that these trial proceedings are still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And, again, on page 8 of your report, Dr. Martell, you indicate that Mr. Hadzic expressed his thoughts "in a logical, coherent, and goal-directed fashion with no evidence of formal thought disorder ..." Can you again just explain a little bit more in detail about what you mean here, please.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes. Overall, Mr. Hadzic's verbal abilities, his speaking abilities, are well-preserved despite the brain tumor. He is able to communicate effectively. He is able to understand what is asked of him and respond in an appropriate fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: On page 11 of your report, you indicate that Mr. Hadzic has good reading comprehension. Again, can you explain a little bit more in detail what you mean and perhaps provide an example, please.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes. He was given - I've mentioned it before - the MMPI-2 which is a test for mental illness. It consists of 567 questions, all of which were written in Croatian. He was able to read and understand the questions. And the test has built into it ways to determine if the person taking the test understands the material. This is done by looking for consistency in the way he answers questions. For example, if there's "I loved my father" and he says "true," later in the test if it says "I loved my father," he should answer "true" again. Or if it says "I hate my father," he should answer "false." This would show that is he understanding the content of the questions. His score on that scale was within normal limits, indicating to me that he was able to read and understand the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Again on page 11 of your report you state that Mr. Hadzic gave coherent responses to a complex verbal expression test. And can you just again explain a little bit in more detail what you mean, please.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I think you're talking about the "Cookie Theft" picture?

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Okay. This is a test that we use to look at how someone expresses themselves verbally. They are shown what's essentially a cartoon of a woman in her house washing the dishes as the sink overflows and her little boy on a stepstool reaching for a cookie jar, and the stepstool is teetering over and he's about to fall onto his little sister who is underneath waiting to get a cookie. And so what we're looking for is can the person describe accurately what they see in the picture. And Mr. Hadzic identifies the woman, identifies the boy, but misses the fact that the water is flowing out of the sink and that the stool is teetering over and -- until later when his attention was drawn that, he was unable to identify those facts. But given that lack of attention to the critical details, he was still able to verbally describe what he saw in the picture. He was what we call concrete. He would say: The woman has a dish in his hand. There are two glasses on the sink. There is a cookie jar. So this is very concrete as opposed to the more abstract ideas of there's things going wrong in the story, the water flowing out of the sink and the children falling off the stool.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Just turning to page 14 of your report, Dr. Martell, can you please explain what you mean when you say that one of Mr. Hadzic's strengths is his intact and appropriate social skills?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Certainly. The tumor at this point has not greatly affected the frontal lobes of his brain. The frontal lobes are the largest part of our brain that are responsible for a lot of our abstract reasoning, critical thinking, decision making, problem solving, and some language functioning. It also monitors our social skills. He is intact with regard to being kind, gracious, understanding what's happening in a situation, behaving appropriately for what's happening in a situation. His social skills therefore are intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: And again on page 14, you refer to Mr. Hadzic's preserved abstract reasoning and abstract problem solving. Can you just discuss this a little bit more, please, and also maybe provide me with a practical example of this?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I administered a couple of tests. One is like a card game where he needs to sort cards to different targets, it might be the number of objects on the card or the colour of the objects on the card or the shape of the objects on the card. So as he sorts, I will tell him if he's right or if he's wrong, say I'm looking for colour. Once he figures out colour, I will say: That's correct, that's correct, that's correct. When he is correct ten times, I don't tell him but I change and now I want to know the number of items on the card. He has to stop sorting to colour and learn what I'm looking for and then start sorting to numbers. And when he gets that right, then I'll change again and go to shapes. So he needs to be able to solve a changing problem situation over time using abstract reasoning skills. He was able to do that without a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Martell, if you just bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, may I please confer with my co-counsel for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Martell, that is all for now from the Prosecution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Martell.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic. I have just a few questions for you today.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I could direct you to page 15 of your report, please, and you were asked some questions about the concept of fitness for trial as you understand it. Can you inform us how you do understand that concept of fitness for trial.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Well, I understand it in the sense of American jurisprudence probably better than I do in terms of the Tribunal's jurisprudence. Certainly in America there's two prongs we look at. One is understanding the charges against him and what happens in the court proceedings is the first prong. The second prong is his capacity to co-operate with counsel and assist in his own defence. I understand that similar standards are applied here. I provided language the best that I had in my report although it was not specified in my referral. It was based from a previous case I did for the Tribunal some years ago. And it's really that second prong of co-operation with counsel and assisting in one's defence that I think is at issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you use this concept in order to identify what cognitive elements or what cognitive performances you were measuring and looking at in Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: In large part, yes. The Court had requested a comprehensive evaluation, so I looked at everything from how fast he can tap his fingers to how smart he is and everything in between but with special attention to those cognitive and mental skills that would be needed in order to participate in a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So those criteria that you understand as being part of fitness for trial were part of your assessment of what skills or cognitive abilities to measure but not an exhaustive description of what you were measuring; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions about potential forms of accommodation of Mr. Hadzic in order to ameliorate his ability to understand. And one of the measures that is possibly available would be for Mr. Hadzic, instead of sitting in the back of the courtroom here and observing the proceedings live, sitting somewhere else and having a screen in front of him with a video of the proceedings going on, perhaps accompanied by a screen, such as the one that you have in front of yourself, showing the words that are spoken in the courtroom. Now, would that kind of arrangement substantially alter, would it make it better, would it make it worse, in terms of the cognitive deficiencies that you've noted on page 15?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: It, if anything, would probably make it worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Because instead of -- when one sits in this room, you have this entire universe of the proceedings to focus your attention upon. When you're sitting on a couch in your house looking at a computer screen and a monitor, you've got your wife, you've got noises in the street, you've got your house, more things to distract you from focusing on what's going on. Plus given his cognitive problems, I doubt that he could attend to, for example, reading words that keep scrolling up on the screen and correlating that with what he is seeing on the video feed. That kind of rapid information processing is a significant deficit area for him. The primary advantage of that arrangement would be that he could stop and rest. The problem would be he would need to notify the Court that he needs to stop and rest, rather than just disengaging or falling asleep while the proceedings are ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In that respect, some terms that we've heard in the past that I noticed did not figure, I believe, in your report are: Executive function --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and suggestibility. And I wonder if you could tell us about Mr. Hadzic's ability to take initiative which I understand is part of executive function.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: It is part of executive function. And by and large his executive functioning is intact. Where he has problems goes to stamina and the ability to maintain attention over time. For example, I gave him a test where he needed to tell me as many words that would start with the letter, like the letter A, and he would start off quite rapidly generating several words in the first 15 seconds of the minute and then slowly stop and go silent for the remaining time. He couldn't maintain the initiative in the process. It's that kind of concern, that inability to maintain focus that is an executive deficit that concerns me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you say over time in response to the answer that -- in your response that you just gave, that's not a time-period of an hour, 30 minutes, 15 minutes. It can be as short as a minute. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you very much. That completes our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Martell, thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] Dr. Martell, thank you very much for coming here and making this deposition. I have two small questions for you in order to understand you clearly. Did you have a chance to find out whether during the tests the accused - or the patient, should I call him - was under the effect of medication? Was he taking any medication that may have affected or impaired his capability to answer your questions?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: He was taking medication, primarily medications for his cancer treatment which are outside of my understanding as a mental health professional. I don't prescribe such medications so it's difficult for me to opine about the effect of those medications on his cognitive ability. I can't rule it out. I know that he described one medicine that he takes at bedtime that helps him to sleep. Whether he takes that during the day, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. I understand, then, that based on the question of whether he takes medication or doesn't take some medication, his capability to answer your questions may vary and it may also impact his capability to participate in his trial. Would that be your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: In general, yes. Psychiatric medications tend to improve a person's performance on neuropsychological tests. You do better with the medication than without it. However, as I said, I'm not as familiar with the chemotherapy medications, and I certainly wouldn't advise him to stop his medications in order to participate in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, thank you very much, indeed. I may put the rest of my questions to the other specialists on this very point. But my second question to you is the following. You explained to the accused - or to your patient, should I put it - the purpose of your tests, the reason why you were running these tests. You wanted to check whether he was fit for trial, to participate actively in his trial. Now, what I would like to know applies not only to this particular patient but I would like to have a more general answer from you. Is it possible for someone who undergoes these very same tests to provide with you false responses to change the results of the tests?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible, and this is a big concern in forensic practice, which is my speciality area. Because of the concern about -- we use the term "malingering" or "faking." Because of that concern, I administered tests mixed in with the regular tests to catch him if he is trying to exaggerate his problems or fake brain damage or fatigue that he does not actually have. Mr. Hadzic in every case passed those tests, indicating he was giving good effort and not exaggerating his problems and, therefore, I believe my findings are reliable and valid indications of his current level of functioning and not the product of manipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you again for your answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Dr. Martell, I have a few questions for you as well. First one is about the qualification of Mr. Hadzic's disease. It is, I read in your report, multi-focal glioblastoma multiforme. Could you please give us a short explanation about the two words "multi-focal" and "multiforme" and the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Multi-focal means that it exists in more than one place at the same time. Glioblastoma multiforme is the classic term for the tumour. The multi-focal is an indication that it has, in fact, metastasized to multiple locations within his brain. I took the phrase directly from the medical reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is about premorbid intelligence. Could you give us a short explanation of what premorbid intelligence is and how it's measured.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I would be glad to. We use the term "premorbid" to indicate what his IQ was before the brain tumour infected him. Given that no one tested his IQ earlier in life, the only way to estimate what it would be is to use a formula, an actuarial formula somewhat like what life insurance companies use to determine how long you will live. It takes into account one's sex, one's age, one's occupation, whether one lives in an urban or a rural setting, and uses these as predictors to provide both a verbal IQ, a performance IQ, and a full-scale IQ estimate. It is only an estimate, but it struck me after the testing I did, given his history, that an IQ of 95 was probably an underestimate of what his true IQ would have been. Hence, I did the -- it's called the Barona Index which was a method to try and estimate what his true IQ would have been before the brain tumour. And it comes out much higher, closer to 120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see that, indeed, Dr. Martell. And your result is approximately 119. It's quite a precise outcome for an estimation based on a demographic formula. I would rather expect a range than a figure. Would you -- wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Yes, I could provided a range. I did not do that in this case because I felt sometimes too much information is not helpful to the Court. But it is possible to calculate those ranges, and if the Court would like, I have what I need to do it here with me, not on the stand but in the waiting him, and I could provide those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I've seen for the Barona Test a range from 20 to 25 IQ points. Would that be reasonable?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I think that plus or minus ten is reasonable, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that's my final question about this topic. Your 119 could also be read as plus or minus 10?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So it's in the middle of that range?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Hadzic scored at the bottom of 1 percentile in multiple tests, including verbal memory, visual memory, and composite memory. That's page 10 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: At what percentile would these impairments manifest themselves to a layman?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I think if one lived with Mr. Hadzic, you'd be quite aware of the impairments that he has, where he will not remember something he told you that morning, where he will not remember something you just watched on television. It may well be something that is apparent to his counsel. So one need not be as impaired as he is for people to notice that level of impairment but certainly anyone -- when you're one out of 100 that's impaired as he is, others will certainly notice it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic's brain tumour is described as rapidly progressive. What does "rapidly progressive" mean exactly? Does it mean that Hadzic's capacity to -- capacities are expected to diminish further; and if they are expected to diminish further, in what way are they expected to do so?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: It's a difficult question to answer. Rapidly progressively means, as it sounds, it gets worse quickly. It grows, it is the most aggressive brain tumour, brain cancer, that one can have. It grew in size just during the time from when he began his chemotherapy until, I think, last November. I have to recall the dates, I'm a little jet-lagged. But it is rapidly growing, and because of that, it can be expected to continue to grow and his capacity to participate will continue to deteriorate. He will get worse. The nature in which he gets worse depends on where the tumour goes. At this point his frontal lobes are fairly well preserved, his language centres are fairly well preserved, but if the tumour begins to invade the language centres or the executive control centres, then there will be further deterioration in those behaviours on top of the ones that are already impaired involving attention, concentration, and memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no follow-up questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I just have a couple of follow-up questions if that's okay with Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Martell, I have just two more questions if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: You mention -- just in relation to the questions, both oral and written, that you asked Mr. Hadzic, you mention that in one afternoon he completed over 500 written questions. Is it correct that you completed those 500-plus, I think you mentioned 547, he completed those questions in one afternoon?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I believe he did that in one afternoon and evening. They are single questions with a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And again, just when you were discussing the oral questions you put to Mr. Hadzic you mentioned that you had asked him hundreds of question and when I asked you did he understand your questions you said, yes, he did and that he was responsive. Can I just -- but in terms of a percentage, would that mean that he understood about 100 per cent of the questions that you asked him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Dr. Martell.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL MARTELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SPELMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If nothing else, Dr. Martell, this hearing comes to an end. We thank you again for assisting the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. We wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there's nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just one, perhaps, procedural matter. We note that in the original order from Your Honours in respect of written submissions following the hearings, you'd indicated that you would want written submissions within four days of the examination of the witnesses. In view of the fact that the second witness will now be delayed, perhaps we could clarify whether Your Honours intend the written submissions to follow four days after the testimony of the second witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Jarvis, as we understand that part of the OTP team, or if not the entire OTP team, is not -- I mean, OTP team in Hadzic case, the normal members of it, are not available right now, it is perhaps better to wait for the submissions until we have had the second expert as well. Would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you. That would certainly seem to make sense in terms of being able to then address the full range of issues in one set of submissions. Your Honours, perhaps I could also just ask whether there is any indication of when the examination of Dr. Specenier will be scheduled, if you know that, at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, without being completely sure but there is an indication it would be, if I'm not wrong, on the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.03 a.m.,
